newsitem.title: ITALY: Govt-trade union talks start on Italian pensions.
newsitem.headline: Govt-trade union talks start on Italian pensions.

text.p: Talks got under way between the centre-left government and trades unions on Tuesday aimed at reforming Italy's unwieldy pensions system, political sources said.
Labour Minister Tiziano Treu, who attended the talks, told reporters on Monday that cuts in pension spending of about five trillion lire ($3 billion) "could be realistic".
But cuts are deeply opposed by the hard-left Communist Refoundation party whose support gives Prime Minister Romano Prodi a majority in parliament.
The sources said the leaders of Italy's three main trades union confederations, Sergio Cofferati of Cgil, Sergio D'Antoni of Cisl and Pietro Larizza of Uil were present at Tuesday's talks.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, Regional Affairs Minister Franco Bassanini and Social Affairs Minister Livia Turco were present, along with cabinet undersecretary Enrico Micheli.
Larizza said he would oppose any cuts in length of service pensions or an extension of contributions.
The government was also due to begin bilateral pensions talks with employers' group Confindustria later on Tuesday.
The talks are the first time the thorny issue of pension reform has been addressed in detail since negotiations on streamlining the welfare state were launched a month ago.

Italy is under pressure to carry out a convincing reform of social spending and to shake up its pensions system to prove that public finances will be kept under control before the planned 1999 launch of the single European currency.
The welfare talks, officially launched in June but which only got under way properly earlier this month, immediately ran into trouble over Italy's generous early retirement system.
The system allows Italians to draw a pension based on the length of service even before they have reach mandatory retirement age.
Trades unions agree that the welfare system should be changed, but they want reforms to focus on providing employment and unemployment benefits.

Prodi said in June that state spending on pensions is some 15 trillion lire a year over budget and needs bringing into line. The government says the aim is to rebalance spending, rather than implement cuts.
